newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Gore, Gingrich to put spotlight on Korean peace.
newsitem.headline: Gore, Gingrich to put spotlight on Korean peace.

text.p: A flurry of U.S. visitors to South Korea this week, including Vice President Al Gore, will put the spotlight on efforts to bring North Korea into peace talks using food aid as leverage.
Gore, who arrives on Friday, and U.S. House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich, due on Monday at the head of a 12-member congressional delegation, will tackle a host of thorny trade issues.

But North Korea will top their agendas amid signs that Pyongyang, desperate for food as famine looms, is ready to enter peace talks proposed last April by U.S. President Bill Clinton and his South Korean counterpart, Kim Young-sam.
"Issues surrounding North and South Korea will be a focal point," said Seoul's Deputy Foreign Minister Song Young-shik.

Separately, five U.S. senators led by Alaska Republican Ted Stevens, chairman of the Senate Appropriations Committee, will stop in Seoul on Thursday on their way to Pyongyang for talks on Friday with North Korean officials.
U.S. and South Korean representatives emerged guardedly optimistic from meetings with North Korean diplomats in New York this month for a briefing on the peace talks, which would also include China.
The U.S. and its close ally South Korea are partners in a delicate mission to forge a permanent peace mechanism to replace a truce that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
Yet their relationship is dogged by mistrust over approaches on handling Pyongyang.
Seoul frets that Washington will cave in too easily to Pyongyang's pleas for food and diplomatic recognition, leaving South Korea feeling ignored and isolated.

Washington officials privately complain that Seoul's uneven policy on the North -- by turns belligerent and conciliatory -- adds to the frustration of engaging Pyongyang in dialogue over issues from missile proliferation to nuclear arms.
The United States maintains 37,000 troops in South Korea guarding the world's last Cold War border -- what U.S. forces call "Freedom's Frontier".

"The U.S. thinks that by sending aid to North Korea it can change Pyongyang's policies, but we don't think North Korea will follow just because you give it candy," said Koo Youngnok, a professor of politics at Seoul National University.
He said North Korea has all along tried to isolate South Korea and deal directly with the United States.
"Unfortunately, the U.S. -- which is in a position to strongly suggest North Korea talk directly to South Korea -- has not made that effort."
The United States has agreed to chip in $10 million and South Korea $6 million to the latest international food appeal for North Korea.
The modest aid is a down-payment on substantial relief Pyongyang could expect if it moved towards peace. U.N. food agencies believe famine in the North is just weeks away.

On the trade front, friction between Washington and Seoul has been exacerbated by South Korean austerity measures put in place as its economy slows. U.S. companies complain that the government is shutting out Western imports -- everything from cars to spirits -- in its drive against luxury spending.
The South Korean government angrily denies sponsoring an anti-import campaign.
Gingrich and his congressional team are visiting South Korea as part of an Asian trip that will also include China, Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan.
Gore is spending two days in South Korea on Friday and Saturday.
The five-member senate team heading to Pyongyang also includes Hawaii Democratic Daniel Inouye and Republicans Pete Domenici of New Mexico, Thad Cochran of Mississippi and Pat Roberts of Kansas.
